questions.question: A permutation matrix is a square matrix with exactly one entry $1$ in each row and each column and zeros elsewhere; a real $n\times n$ matrix $Q$ is orthogonal if $Q^{\top}Q=I$. Which statement about permutation matrices is correct?
options: Only the identity matrix is both a permutation matrix and orthogonal
A permutation matrix is orthogonal only if it is symmetric
Every permutation matrix is orthogonal
A permutation matrix with determinant $-1$ is not orthogonal

questions.question: Recall that a real $n\times n$ matrix $Q$ is orthogonal if $Q^{\top}Q=I$. Which statement about the determinant and orthogonality is correct?
options: Every orthogonal matrix has determinant $1$, as rotations do
Orthogonal implies $\det Q=\pm1$, but not conversely
A square matrix with determinant $\pm1$ is always orthogonal
An orthogonal matrix can have any nonzero determinant

questions.question: Let $Q$ be a real $3\times2$ matrix whose two columns are orthonormal in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Recall that a real $n\times n$ matrix is called orthogonal if $Q^{\top}Q=I$. Which statement about $Q$ is correct?
options: $Q^{\top}Q=I_2$, $QQ^{\top}\neq I_3$; $Q$ is not called orthogonal
$Q$ is an orthogonal matrix, because it satisfies $Q^{\top}Q=I_2$
$QQ^{\top}=I_3$ as well, because $Q^{\top}$ is an inverse of $Q$
The rows of $Q$ are orthonormal, just like its columns

questions.question: Recall that a real $n\times n$ matrix $Q$ is orthogonal if $Q^{\top}Q=I$. Which of these $2\times2$ matrices is orthogonal?
options: $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&\tfrac{1}{2}\end{pmatrix}$
$\tfrac{1}{5}\begin{pmatrix}3&-4\\4&3\end{pmatrix}$
$\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$

questions.question: The matrix $Q=\tfrac{1}{13}\begin{pmatrix}5&12\\-12&5\end{pmatrix}$ satisfies $Q^{\top}Q=I$. What is $Q^{-1}$?
options: $\tfrac{1}{13}\begin{pmatrix}5&12\\-12&5\end{pmatrix}$
$\tfrac{1}{13}\begin{pmatrix}-5&-12\\12&-5\end{pmatrix}$
$13\begin{pmatrix}5&-12\\12&5\end{pmatrix}$
$\tfrac{1}{13}\begin{pmatrix}5&-12\\12&5\end{pmatrix}$

questions.question: The matrix $R=\tfrac{1}{5}\begin{pmatrix}3&-4\\4&3\end{pmatrix}$ satisfies $R^{\top}R=I$. Which vector $\boldsymbol{x}$ solves $R\boldsymbol{x}=(5,0)^{\top}$?
The matrix $S=\tfrac{1}{5}\begin{pmatrix}3&4\\4&-3\end{pmatrix}$ is orthogonal. What is $\det S$, and what kind of map is $\boldsymbol{x}\mapsto S\boldsymbol{x}$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$?
options: $\det S=-1$; a reflection in a line through the origin
$\det S=1$; a rotation about the origin by an acute angle
$\det S=-25$; so $S$ is not orthogonal after all
$\det S=1$; a reflection, because $S$ is symmetric

questions.question: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ and recall that a real $n\times n$ matrix $Q$ is orthogonal if $Q^{\top}Q=I$. For which real numbers $c$ is $cA$ orthogonal?
options: $c=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ only
No $c$ works, since $\det A=-2$
$c=\pm\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

questions.question: Recall that a real $n\times n$ matrix $Q$ is orthogonal if $Q^{\top}Q=I$. Which real numbers can occur as a real eigenvalue $\lambda$ of an orthogonal matrix (with a real eigenvector $\boldsymbol{p}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$, $Q\boldsymbol{p}=\lambda\boldsymbol{p}$)?
options: Any real $\lambda$ with $|\lambda|\le1$
Only $\lambda=1$
Only $\lambda=1$ and $\lambda=-1$
Any real $\lambda\neq0$, since $Q$ is invertible

questions.question: Let $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ be orthogonal $n\times n$ matrices, where a real $n\times n$ matrix $Q$ is orthogonal if $Q^{\top}Q=I$. Which matrix is orthogonal for every such choice of $Q_1$ and $Q_2$?
Recall that a real $n\times n$ matrix $Q$ is orthogonal if $Q^{\top}Q=I$. For which $(a,b)$ is $Q=\begin{pmatrix}\tfrac{3}{5}&a\\\tfrac{4}{5}&b\end{pmatrix}$ orthogonal with $\det Q=-1$?

Recall that a real $n\times n$ matrix $Q$ is orthogonal if $Q^{\top}Q=I$. Some orthogonal $3\times3$ matrix $Q$ maps $\boldsymbol{x}=(2,3,6)^{\top}$ to $Q\boldsymbol{x}=(6,2,a)^{\top}$. Which values of the real number $a$ are possible?
options: $a=3$ only
$a=\sqrt{89}$ or $a=-\sqrt{89}$

questions.question: Recall that a real $n\times n$ matrix $Q$ is orthogonal if $Q^{\top}Q=I$. Which statement about the (possibly complex) eigenvalues of real square matrices and orthogonality is correct?
options: A real matrix whose eigenvalues all have modulus $1$ is orthogonal
Every orthogonal matrix has at least one real eigenvalue, $1$ or $-1$
Every orthogonal matrix has $n$ real eigenvalues, each $1$ or $-1$
Orthogonal forces $|\lambda|=1$ for each eigenvalue, but not conversely

questions.question: A real $n\times n$ matrix $Q$ satisfies $Q^{\top}Q=I$. Which argument shows that then also $QQ^{\top}=I$?
options: $(\det Q)^2=1$, so $Q$ is invertible and $Q^{-1}=Q^{\top}$
$Q^{\top}Q$ and $QQ^{\top}$ are equal for every square matrix
$Q^{\top}Q=I$ forces $Q$ to be symmetric, so $QQ^{\top}=Q^{\top}Q$
$\det(Q^{\top}Q)=1$, and a determinant of $1$ makes a product equal to $I$

questions.question: A real $2\times2$ matrix $A$ has unit columns, $\|A\boldsymbol{e}_1\|=\|A\boldsymbol{e}_2\|=1$, and satisfies $\|A(\boldsymbol{e}_1+\boldsymbol{e}_2)\|=1$ (dot product norm). What is $(A\boldsymbol{e}_1)\cdot(A\boldsymbol{e}_2)$, and is $A$ orthogonal ($A^{\top}A=I$)?
options: It is $-1$, so $A$ is not orthogonal
It is $-\tfrac{1}{2}$, so $A$ is not orthogonal
It is $0$, so $A$ is an orthogonal matrix
It is $+\tfrac{1}{2}$, so $A$ is not orthogonal

questions.question: A real $n\times n$ matrix $Q$ with columns $\boldsymbol{q}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{q}_n$ is called orthogonal if $Q^{\top}Q=I$. Which condition on the columns is equivalent to $Q^{\top}Q=I$, using the dot product on $\mathbb{R}^n$?
options: They are orthonormal: orthogonal and of norm $1$
They are pairwise orthogonal, with any nonzero lengths
Each has norm $1$, at any angles to one another
They are linearly independent, so that $Q$ is invertible

questions.question: Recall that a real $n\times n$ matrix $Q$ is orthogonal if $Q^{\top}Q=I$. Which description fits the map $\boldsymbol{x}\mapsto Q\boldsymbol{x}$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the dot product?
options: It preserves lengths, but in general changes angles between vectors
It keeps every vector on its own line through the origin
It preserves angles, but multiplies every length by a common factor $c\neq1$
It preserves lengths, distances and angles between vectors

questions.question: Recall that a real $n\times n$ matrix $Q$ is orthogonal if $Q^{\top}Q=I$. Which description covers exactly the maps $\boldsymbol{x}\mapsto Q\boldsymbol{x}$ given by orthogonal $2\times2$ matrices $Q$?
options: Only the rotations of the plane about the origin
Rotations about the origin and reflections in lines through it
The rotations, the reflections and also the uniform scalings by $c\neq0$
All rigid motions of the plane, including translations

questions.question: Let $S_1=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ (the reflection in the $x_1$-axis) and $S_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ (the reflection in the line $x_2=x_1$). Which map is $\boldsymbol{x}\mapsto S_2S_1\boldsymbol{x}$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$?
options: A reflection, since both factors are reflections
The rotation about the origin by $45^\circ$
The rotation about the origin by $90^\circ$
The identity, since each reflection undoes itself
